steps.body: A zero added after the last decimal digit changes nothing: 0.60 and 0.6 shade exactly the same six columns.
steps.narration: A zero added after the last decimal digit changes nothing: 0.60 and 0.6 shade exactly the same six columns.

widget.prompt: Shade the grid to show 0.60. Each full column is one tenth; each cell is one hundredth.

commonCounts.feedback: That shades 6 single cells — 0.06. Both 0.6 and 0.60 mean six full columns; the trailing zero adds no cells.

widget.successFeedback: Six full columns — 60 cells. 0.60 and 0.6 shade exactly the same amount.
widget.lowFeedback: The shaded amount is still below the target. Fill whole columns for the tenths digit first, then single cells for the hundredths.
widget.highFeedback: The shaded amount has gone past the target. Each full column is one tenth — check the tenths digit before adding single cells.

predict.prompt: Is 0.60 more than, less than, or the same as 0.6?
predict.reveal: 0.60 is 60 hundredths and 0.6 is 6 tenths — six full columns either way. A zero tacked on after the last decimal digit adds nothing — though after a whole number like 6, a zero would make 60.

explanationVariants: Compare tenths first, then hundredths — the amounts match, so 0.60 = 0.6.

widget.prompt: Compare the two decimals: 0.60 ? 0.6. Choose the relation that holds.
widget.successFeedback: Correct — comparing digit by digit from the tenths place settles it: 0.60 = 0.6.
widget.ltFeedback: Line up the places before deciding: compare the tenths digits of 0.60 and 0.6 first, and only look at hundredths when the tenths tie. Counting digits instead of comparing places points the wrong way here.
widget.gtFeedback: Line up the places before deciding: compare the tenths digits of 0.60 and 0.6 first, and only look at hundredths when the tenths tie. A longer decimal is often the smaller one.
